overview: Dilophosaurus was a large Early Jurassic theropod from Arizona, about six metres long, bearing two thin parallel bony crests along the skull roof. These were display structures — far too fragile for combat — and Dilophosaurus was one of the largest terrestrial predators of its time at ~193 million years ago.

The Jurassic Park portrayal of Dilophosaurus with an expandable neck frill and venom is entirely fictional; no fossil evidence supports either feature. The notch in its upper jaw between the premaxilla and maxilla once led to scavenging hypotheses, since largely refuted by biomechanical analysis.

fossilSites.name: Kayenta Formation
fossilSites.note: Lower Jurassic continental deposits with the type specimen and additional material alongside prosauropods and tritylodontid cynodonts.

articles.title: Discovery and naming
articles.body: Sam Welles first described material from the Kayenta Formation in 1954, initially identifying it as a large Megalosaurus. He renamed it Dilophosaurus wetherilli in 1970, honouring Navajo guide Jesse Wetherbee. A second specimen found in 1964 provided much of the postcranial anatomy known today.

articles.title: Skull crests
articles.body: The twin crests run from the snout to above the orbits, formed by the nasal bones. Their paper-thin construction rules out a weapon function. Analogous thin cranial crests in other theropods (Oviraptor, Guanlong) and in cassowaries are consistently associated with display and species recognition.

articles.title: Ecology
articles.body: Dilophosaurus represents a transitional grade between small coelophysoids and the larger tetanurans that dominated the Jurassic. In the Kayenta Formation it coexisted with the prosauropod Massospondylus and early crocodylomorphs in a seasonally arid environment, probably pursuing medium-sized prey.

fossilRecord.material: Several skeletons with skull material from Early Jurassic deposits.
fossilRecord.paleo: Early Jurassic fluvial and floodplain environments in western North America.
fossilRecord.evidence: Paired skull crests and theropod skeletal anatomy distinguish it from later movie-inspired reconstructions.

record.description: Dilophosaurus wetherilli was a large early theropod from the Kayenta Formation of Arizona. Several partial skeletons, including substantial skull material, document paired cranial crests and a powerful bipedal predator very unlike its fictionalised venom-spitting portrayal.
facts: There is no fossil evidence for venom glands or an expandable neck frill.
The paired crests were thin and probably visual structures, though their exact function is unknown.
Modern re-preparation shows a more robust skull and skeleton than older weak-jawed reconstructions.

review.ageReviewNote: U-Pb dating places the fossil-bearing Kayenta interval near 193 Ma in the Sinemurian.
